title: Two-way (contingency) table
body: A two-way table, also called a contingency table, summarizes data for two categorical variables, with cells holding frequencies (counts) or relative frequencies (proportions).
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.1 "A two-way table, also called a contingency table"

title: Graphs for two categorical variables
body: Three graphs display the relationship between two categorical variables by showing the frequency or relative frequency of each level of one variable within each category of the other.

items.label: Side-by-side bar chart
items.meaning: Bars for the levels of one variable are shown for each category of the other variable.

items.label: Segmented bar chart
items.meaning: One bar per category of a variable, divided into segments for the levels of the other variable.

items.label: Mosaic plot
items.meaning: Displays the frequency or relative frequency of each level of one variable across the categories of the other variable.

ced_evidence: 2.1.A.2 "Side-by-side bar charts, segmented bar charts, and mosaic plots"

title: Judging association from two categorical variables
body: Compare the distribution of one categorical variable across the levels of the other (using graphs or summary statistics) to decide whether the two variables are associated, and use that evidence to justify claims in context.
ced_evidence: 2.1.A.3 "determine whether the two variables are associated"; 2.2.B.1

title: Joint relative frequency
body: \text{joint relative frequency}=\frac{\text{cell frequency}}{\text{total for the entire table}}
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.1 "cell frequency divided by the total for the entire table"

title: Marginal relative frequency
body: \text{marginal relative frequency}=\frac{\text{row total (or column total)}}{\text{total for the entire table}}
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.2 "a row total divided by the total for the entire table or a column total divided by the total for the entire table"

title: Conditional relative frequency
body: \text{conditional relative frequency}=\frac{\text{cell frequency in a row}}{\text{total for that row}}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{\text{cell frequency in a column}}{\text{total for that column}}
ced_evidence: 2.2.A.3 "a cell frequency in a row divided by the total for that row"

title: Random process, outcome, and event
body: A random process generates results determined by chance, an outcome is the result of one trial of a random process, and an event is a collection of outcomes.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.1-2.3.A.3 "An event is a collection of outcomes"

title: Probability as long-run relative frequency
body: The probability of an outcome or event is its long-run relative frequency, meaning its relative frequency over a large number of trials, and the relative frequency from empirical data estimates the true probability.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.5 "long-run relative frequency"; 2.3.A.6

title: Law of large numbers
body: For independent trials, as the number of trials increases, the long-run relative frequency of an outcome or event gets closer and closer to a single value.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.7 "The law of large numbers states"

title: Simulation to estimate probabilities
body: In a simulation, associate every possible outcome with a value determined by chance, record the counts of simulated outcomes and the total count, and use the relative frequency to estimate the probability.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.4 "Record the counts of simulated outcomes and the count total"; 2.10.D.1

title: Sample space
body: The sample space of a random process is the set of all possible nonoverlapping outcomes, and its probability is 1.
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.1 "the set of all possible nonoverlapping outcomes"

title: Theoretical probability (equally likely outcomes)
body: P(E)=\frac{\text{number of outcomes in event }E}{\text{total number of outcomes in the sample space}}
caution: Applies only when all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely.
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.2 "If all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely"

title: Range of a probability
body: The probability of an event is a number between 0 and 1, inclusive.
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.3 "between 0 and 1, inclusive"

title: Complement rule
ced_evidence: 2.4.A.4 "equal to 1 - P(E)"

title: Joint probability
body: The joint probability that events A and B both occur is the probability of the intersection of A and B, written P(A ∩ B).
ced_evidence: 2.5.A.1 "Joint probability is defined as P(A ∩ B)"

title: Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events
body: A \text{ and } B \text{ mutually exclusive} \Rightarrow P(A\cap B)=0
ced_evidence: 2.5.A.2 "if two events are mutually exclusive, then P(A ∩ B) = 0"

title: Conditional probability
body: P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}
ced_evidence: 2.6.A.1 "Conditional probability is defined as"

title: General multiplication rule
body: P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B\mid A)
ced_evidence: 2.6.A.2 "The multiplication rule is defined as"

title: Independent events
body: A,B\text{ independent}\iff P(A\mid B)=P(A),\; P(B\mid A)=P(B),\; P(A\cap B)=P(A)\cdot P(B)
caution: Independence means knowing one event occurred does not change the other's probability. Do not default to a without-replacement (dependent) calculation when the events are independent.
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.1 "independent if and only if knowing whether event A has occurred"

title: Union of two events (addition rule)
body: P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)

title: Random variable
body: A random variable is a variable whose values are numerical outcomes of a random phenomenon.
ced_evidence: 2.8.A.1 "A random variable is a variable whose values have numerical outcomes"

title: Valid discrete probability distribution
body: A discrete probability distribution gives the probability of every possible value of the random variable (as a graph, table, or function), and these probabilities sum to 1.
ced_evidence: 2.8.A.2 "The sum of the probabilities over all possible values of a discrete random variable is 1"

title: Cumulative probability distribution
body: A cumulative probability distribution, given as a table or function, shows the probability of being less than or equal to each value of the discrete random variable.
caution: Watch boundary inclusion: "fewer than 3" is P(X ≤ 2), not P(X ≤ 3).
ced_evidence: 2.8.A.5 "less than or equal to each value"

title: Parameter
body: A parameter is a numerical value measuring a characteristic of a probability distribution or population, and it is a single, fixed value.
ced_evidence: 2.9.A.1 "is a parameter. The value of a parameter is a single, fixed value"

title: Mean (expected value) of a discrete random variable
body: \mu_X=E(X)=\sum x_i\cdot P(x_i)
caution: Each value must be weighted by its probability; the unweighted average of the possible values is not the expected value. Interpret it as the long-run average outcome, in context.

title: Standard deviation of a discrete random variable
body: \sigma_X=\sqrt{\sum (x_i-\mu_X)^2\cdot P(x_i)}
caution: Interpret it as the typical deviation of the values from the mean over the long run, in context and with units.

title: Variance of a random variable
body: V(X)=\sigma_X^{2}
ced_evidence: 2.9.A.3 "The square of the standard deviation ... is called the variance"

title: Conditions for a binomial random variable
body: A binomial random variable counts successes in repeated trials that meet these conditions.

items.label: Two outcomes
items.meaning: Each trial has only two possible outcomes, success or failure.

items.label: Fixed n
items.meaning: There is a fixed number of trials, n.

items.label: Constant p
items.meaning: The probability of success p is the same on every trial, and the probability of failure is 1 − p.

caution: Define X as a count in context (e.g., the number of rock songs played in one hour) and name the distribution binomial with stated n and p. A binomial count is not normally distributed.
ced_evidence: 2.10.A.1 "counts the number of successes in repeated independent trials, n"

expands_to.means: Same probability of success each trial

hooks.when_to_use: When justifying why a random variable is or is not binomial.

title: Binomial probability function
body: P(X=x)=\binom{n}{x}p^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},\quad x=0,1,2,\ldots,n
caution: If calculator syntax is used, label n and p in words.
ced_evidence: 2.10.E.1 "This is called the binomial probability function"

title: Mean of a binomial distribution
body: \mu_X=np
ced_evidence: 2.10.B.1 "its mean, μX, is np"

title: Standard deviation of a binomial distribution
body: \sigma_X=\sqrt{np(1-p)}
ced_evidence: 2.10.B.1 "its standard deviation, σX, is √np(1-p)"

title: Continuous random variable
body: A continuous random variable can take on any value within a specified domain, and every interval within the domain has a probability associated with it.
ced_evidence: 2.11.A.1 "can take on any value within a specified domain"

title: Normal distribution
body: A normal distribution is a continuous, unimodal, bell-shaped, symmetric curve identified by its mean μ and standard deviation σ.
caution: A smaller σ gives a taller, more concentrated curve around the mean; a larger σ gives a shorter, less concentrated curve.
ced_evidence: 2.11.A.3, 2.11.A.5 "identified by two parameters, the mean, µ, and the standard deviation, σ"

title: Standard normal distribution
body: A standard normal distribution is a normal distribution with mean μ = 0 and standard deviation σ = 1.
ced_evidence: 2.11.B.1 "mean μ = 0 and standard deviation σ = 1"

title: Empirical rule (68–95–99.7 rule)
body: For a normal distribution, approximate percentages of observations lie within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean.
ced_evidence: 2.11.C.1 "approximately 68% ... approximately 95% ... approximately 99.7%"

title: Probability as area under the normal curve
body: For an approximately normal random variable, the probability of an interval equals the area under the curve over that interval, and the total area is 1.
ced_evidence: 2.11.D.1 "determined by the area under the normal curve within that interval"

title: Interval notation for normal areas (p is a percentage)
body: P(X<x_a)=p/100 means the lowest p% lie left of x_a, P(x_a<X<x_b)=p/100 means p% lie between, P(X>x_b)=p/100 means the highest p% lie right of x_b, and the most extreme p% on both sides splits into p/200 in each tail.
caution: Here p is a number between 0 and 100 (a percentage), not a proportion; boundaries can be found with technology or with z-scores and a standard normal table.
ced_evidence: 2.11.E.2.i-iv "p is defined as a number between 0 and 100"

title: Comparing relative position in normal distributions
body: Percentiles and proportions can be used to compare the relative positions of individual values within a normal distribution or between normal distributions.
ced_evidence: 2.11.F.1 "Percentiles and proportions may be used to compare relative positions"

title: Sampling distribution
body: The sampling distribution of a statistic is the distribution of values of the statistic for all possible samples of a given size from a given population.
ced_evidence: 2.12.A.1 "distribution of values of the statistic for all possible samples of a given size"

title: Simulating a sampling distribution
body: Steps to approximate a sampling distribution by simulation.

items.meaning: Repeatedly generate a large number of random samples from the population, assuming known value(s) for the parameter(s).
Determine and record the value of the statistic for each sample.
The resulting distribution of statistic values approximates the sampling distribution of the statistic.

ced_evidence: 2.12.A.2 "repeatedly generating a large number of random samples"

title: Randomization distribution
body: A randomization distribution is the distribution of a statistic generated by simulation from repeatedly randomly reallocating the response values to treatment groups and recording the statistic each time.
ced_evidence: 2.12.A.3 "randomly reallocating, or reassigning, the response values to treatment groups"

title: Central limit theorem (CLT)
body: The central limit theorem states that the sampling distribution of a mean of a random sample has a shape that can be approximated by a normal distribution, and the larger the sample, the better the approximation.
ced_evidence: 2.12.A.4 "The central limit theorem (CLT) states"
